title: Community and population ecology
summary: How do populations grow, and how do species live together?
cards.0.p: Individuals of the same species living in an area form a population. The number of individuals per unit area is the density. Individuals can be distributed in a clumped, uniform or random pattern.
cards.0.key: The most common distribution in nature is clumped. Uniform distribution results from territory defense or competition, while random distribution appears when resources are equal everywhere.
cards.1.p: The base of an age pyramid shows the young. In an expanding pyramid the population grows, in a stable pyramid it stays constant, and in a contracting pyramid it shrinks. The sex ratio also affects reproductive power.
cards.1.svg#0: left: male · right: female · bottom: young, top: old
cards.1.svg#7: the number of pre-reproductive young sets the future
cards.1.key: The base of the pyramid shows the population's future. A high share of young people means the population will grow.
cards.1.once.soru: A country has far more children than elderly people. How will its population change?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: The many young people will have children later. So the population grows.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: With few young people the population would shrink, but here there are many.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: If the age groups were similar in size, the population would stay constant.
cards.2.p: Births and immigration increase a population, while deaths and emigration decrease it. In a closed population with no migration, only births and deaths set its size.
cards.2.key: If births plus immigrants equal deaths plus emigrants, the population size does not change.
cards.3.h: Growth: J curve and S curve
cards.3.p: With unlimited resources, a population grows at a constant rate and forms a J curve. In nature, environmental resistance slows growth. The population levels off at the carrying capacity (K) and forms an S curve.
cards.3.key: An organism's maximum reproductive power is called its biotic potential. K is the largest number of individuals the environment can support. The J curve doesn't last long in nature.
cards.4.p: The effect of density-dependent factors such as competition, epidemics and predation grows as crowding increases. Density-independent factors such as frost, drought, floods and fires act regardless of crowding.
cards.4.key: The main brake that keeps a population near its carrying capacity (K) is density-dependent factors.
cards.5.p: r-strategists have many small offspring, give them no care and live short lives. Insects are an example. K-strategists have few offspring, care for them and live long. Like elephants, their numbers stay close to K.
cards.5.svg#17: r: multiply fast · K: stay at K
cards.5.key: r-strategists multiply quickly in changing environments. They are often the first to settle after a fire or in a new pond.
cards.5.once.soru: A fish lays thousands of eggs but does not care for its young. An elephant cares for its single calf for years. Which loses most of its offspring?
cards.5.once.secenekler.0.neden: Most young without care die. The large number of eggs makes up for this loss.
cards.5.once.secenekler.1.neden: The elephant protects its calf, and the calf's chance of survival is high.
cards.5.once.secenekler.2.neden: Care greatly raises the offspring's chance of survival.
cards.6.p: A survivorship curve shows how many individuals are alive at each age. In Type I, deaths happen in old age, and in Type II they happen at an equal rate at every age. In Type III, deaths are concentrated among the young.
cards.6.key: Humans and elephants are Type I, some birds are Type II, and fish and frogs are Type III.
cards.6.once.soru: At what stage do most people die today?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: Thanks to care and medicine, most people live until old age.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: Infant deaths have dropped sharply today.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: The death rate rises clearly in old age.
cards.7.h: Niche and the competitive exclusion principle
cards.7.p: All the populations in an area form a community. Each species has a niche, or role, in the community. Two species that use the same limited resource in the same way cannot live together for long. This is the principle of competitive exclusion.
cards.7.svg#6: In separate jars, both grow along an S curve.
cards.7.svg#7: When they share the same resource, one is excluded.
cards.7.key: Gause's Paramecium experiment demonstrated this principle. Species can separate their niches by choosing different foods, times or areas.
cards.8.p: Intraspecific competition happens between individuals of the same species and is usually the fiercest. Interspecific competition happens between species whose niches overlap. In amensalism, one species is harmed and the other is unaffected.
cards.8.key: Penicillium mold stops bacteria around it from multiplying, and this is amensalism. Intraspecific competition limits a population in a density-dependent way.
cards.8.once.soru: Between which is competition usually fiercest?
cards.8.once.secenekler.0.neden: Members of the same species have identical niches. They compete for the same food and space.
cards.8.once.secenekler.1.neden: The niches of different species only partly overlap.
cards.8.once.secenekler.2.neden: The predator-prey relationship is a feeding relationship, not competition.
cards.9.p: Predator and prey numbers rise and fall in cycles. The predator's numbers peak after the prey's. Predators mostly catch weak individuals and so keep the prey population healthy.
cards.9.svg#4: the predator peaks after the prey
cards.9.key: The predator stops the prey from overmultiplying and using up its own food. Where wolves were wiped out, deer can strip the vegetation.
cards.10.p: In symbiosis, two species live closely together. In mutualism, both species benefit, and lichen is an example. In commensalism, one benefits and the other is unaffected. In parasitism, the parasite benefits and the host is harmed.
cards.10.svg#5: two species wanting the same food
cards.10.key: Lichen is a partnership of a fungus and an alga, and mycorrhiza is a partnership of a fungus and a root. The tapeworm is an internal parasite, while fleas and ticks are external parasites. A parasite usually does not kill its host right away.
cards.10.etk.soru: Put each relationship in the right type of symbiosis.
cards.10.etk.ogeler.3.2: The remora feeds on the shark's leftovers, and the shark is unaffected (+/0).
cards.10.etk.ogeler.4.2: The orchid clings to the tree to reach light, but does not take the tree's food. The tree is unaffected (+/0).
cards.10.etk.ogeler.7.2: The tick sucks the host's blood and the host is harmed (+/−). The tick is an external parasite.
cards.10.once.soru: In a lichen, the fungus gives the alga water and shelter, and the alga gives the fungus food. Which one benefits?
cards.10.once.secenekler.0.neden: Each gives what the other cannot provide. This is called mutualism.
cards.10.once.secenekler.1.neden: The alga also benefits from the water and shelter the fungus provides.
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.neden: The fungus also gets the food the alga makes.
cards.11.p: In camouflage, an organism hides by looking like its surroundings. The stick insect and the arctic fox are examples. In mimicry, one species looks like another. For example, the harmless hoverfly has the pattern of a bee.
cards.11.svg#2: stick insect looks like a twig
cards.11.svg#3: arctic fox turns white in winter
cards.11.svg#9: camouflage: look like the setting · mimicry: look like another species
cards.11.key: Camouflage helps both prey and predators. In camouflage the organism resembles its surroundings, and in mimicry it resembles another organism.
cards.11.once.soru: A harmless fly has the yellow-black pattern of a stinging bee. What does this pattern give the fly?
cards.11.once.secenekler.0.neden: A predator that has been stung by a bee also avoids eating a fly with a similar pattern.
cards.11.once.secenekler.1.neden: The pattern does not give the fly the bee's abilities.
cards.11.once.secenekler.2.neden: Bees recognize the fly. The pattern works against predators.
cards.12.p: In succession, a community is gradually replaced by other communities over time. Primary succession begins with lichens on bare rock without soil. Secondary succession happens where soil remains and is faster. The process ends with a climax community.
cards.12.svg#9: primary: from bare rock, very slow
cards.12.key: Secondary succession happens after a fire or on abandoned fields. The difference is the soil. Without soil it is primary succession, and with soil it is secondary.
cards.12.once.soru: Which organisms settle first on a freshly cooled lava flow?
cards.12.once.secenekler.0.neden: Lichens can cling to rock without soil. They wear down the rock and form soil.
cards.12.once.secenekler.1.neden: Trees need soil to put down roots.
cards.12.once.secenekler.2.neden: Grasses also need soil. Lichens prepare the soil first.
cards.13.p: Species diversity depends on the number of species and on how evenly individuals are spread among them. A species that affects the community far more strongly than its numbers suggest is called a keystone species.
cards.13.key: In Paine's experiment, the number of species fell from 15 to 8. A keystone species does not have to be the most numerous, because its effect is larger than its numbers.
cards.13.once.soru: Predatory sea stars were removed from a shore. What happened to the number of species there?
cards.13.once.secenekler.0.neden: Mussels multiplied and covered the rocks. So there was no room left for other species.
cards.13.once.secenekler.1.neden: With the predator gone, one species became dominant and the others found no space.
cards.13.once.secenekler.2.neden: The sea star was a keystone species, and its removal changed the community.
cards.14.p: The human population was 1 billion in 1800. As farming, medicine and clean water reduced deaths, the population grew along a J-like curve and reached 8 billion in 2022. Today the growth rate is falling.
cards.14.key: The world population was 2 billion in 1927 and 4 billion in 1974. The annual growth rate has been falling since the 1960s. Earth's carrying capacity for humans is still debated.
cards.14.once.soru: About how many billion people live on Earth today?
cards.14.once.secenekler.0.neden: The world population passed 8 billion in 2022.
cards.14.once.secenekler.2.neden: The population has not even reached half of this number yet.
cards.15.p:
• Births, deaths and migration change the size of a population.
• Unlimited resources give a J curve and limited resources an S curve. The S curve levels off at K.
• Of two species using the same limited resource, one is excluded.
• Mutualism is +/+, commensalism +/0, parasitism +/− and competition −/−.
• Succession begins with pioneer lichens and settles at a climax.
quiz.0.q: A lake with a carrying capacity (K) of 800 has a fish population growing along an S curve. At what population size is the yearly increase greatest?
quiz.0.e: On an S curve, growth is fastest at K/2, that is, at 800 ÷ 2 = 400 individuals. When the population is smaller, few individuals are reproducing. As it nears K, environmental resistance stops the growth.
quiz.1.q: Group each factor by how it limits a population.
quiz.1.e: The effect of nesting sites, water and contagious disease grows as crowding increases. A hurricane, hail or a volcanic eruption affects a sparse or a dense population at a similar rate.
quiz.2.q: Match each concept with its example.
quiz.2.ciftler.3.1: A hoverfly that looks like a bee
quiz.2.ciftler.4.1: A stick insect that looks like a twig
quiz.2.e: In a lichen, the fungus and the alga both benefit, and this is mutualism. A tick harms its host, and this is parasitism. Penicillium mold inhibits bacteria but is itself unaffected, which is amensalism. A hoverfly resembling a bee is mimicry, and a stick insect hiding by resembling its surroundings is camouflage.
quiz.3.q: A few years after a forest fire, grasses appear first in the burned area, followed by shrubs and young trees. Which is true of this process?
quiz.3.o.2: It is secondary succession and starts with lichens.
quiz.3.o.3: It does not count as succession.
quiz.3.e: The fire destroys the vegetation but leaves the soil. So the process is secondary succession, and the stage of lichens building soil is skipped.
quiz.3.y.1: Because the soil remains, this is secondary succession. A process that starts with lichens happens on bare rock.
quiz.3.y.2: Lichens wearing down rock is specific to primary succession. Here the soil is already present.
quiz.3.y.3: The rebuilding of a disturbed community is secondary succession. The earlier community does not prevent it.
A:ozet: Keep a population steady, compare distributions, build the J and S curves, follow predator and prey and repeat Gause's experiment.
A:adimlar.0.metin: An island has 500 birds. In one year 60 chicks hatch, 80 birds die and 20 birds migrate away. How many birds must arrive from other islands for the number to stay the same?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.ipucu: Births and immigrants increase the number, while deaths and emigrants decrease it. The two bars must be equal.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.tamam: 60 + 40 = 80 + 20. Because the increase equals the decrease, the population stayed at 500.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.soru: In a desert, shrubs compete for water with their roots, and the area around each shrub stays empty. How are these shrubs distributed?
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: In a clumped distribution, individuals gather around a resource. Here each shrub keeps its neighbors away.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Random distribution appears when interactions between individuals are weak. Here there is strong competition.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Competition for resources or territory defense keeps individuals evenly spaced.
A:adimlar.2.metin: A jar with unlimited food holds 10 bacteria, and their number doubles every generation. Step through the generations and find the first one where the number passes 1000.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.ipucu: The number goes 10, 20, 40, 80. Stop at the first generation that crosses the red line.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.tamam: In generation 7, the 10 bacteria reached 1280. Even though the rate stays constant, the number added each generation grows. This is called exponential growth.
A:adimlar.3.metin: Here the carrying capacity is K = 1000. Find the population size at which growth is fastest.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.ipucu: In a small population, few individuals are reproducing. Near K, limiting factors stop the growth. Look for the peak of the lower curve.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.tamam: Growth is fastest around K/2 = 500, where the S curve is steepest. As the population nears K, growth drops to zero. K is not fixed. It changes when the environment changes.
A:adimlar.4.metin: Some factors have a stronger effect as crowding increases, and these are called density-dependent factors. Others ignore crowding, and these are called density-independent factors. Change the density and the event.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.soru: By this measure, what kind of factor is a flood?
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: A flood affects most individuals in the area regardless of crowding. Density-dependent factors are things like epidemics, competition and predation.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Frost, drought, floods and fires affect sparse and dense populations at a similar rate. The test here is whether the effect grows as crowding increases.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: A flood affects populations of any density, and its effect does not depend on density.
A:adimlar.5.metin: In Canada, the numbers of snowshoe hares and the lynx that hunt them were recorded for years. The two populations affect each other. Predict first, then watch.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: When does the lynx population peak?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: When prey multiply, the predator's food increases and the predator multiplies afterward. More predators reduce the prey, and then the predators decline too. This cycle takes about 10 years.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.yazi: At the same time as the hares
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: For the predator to multiply, the prey must multiply first and the young must grow. That takes time.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The predator cannot multiply before its food increases. The predator's rise follows the prey's rise.
A:adimlar.6.metin: Gause fed two Paramecium species the same food. Grow them in separate jars first, then in the same jar.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.soru: Why did P. caudatum die out in the shared jar?
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Both species feed on bacteria, and neither eats the other. The loss comes from competition for food.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.yazi: Both used the same limited food in the same way
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Both species fed on the same bacteria. The faster-growing P. aurelia used up the food, and its rival starved and died out.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.2.yazi: Both declined because the jar was small
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: P. aurelia did not decline. It multiplied and leveled off. Only its rival died out.
A:adimlar.7.metin: Hares (prey) and lynx (predators) live in a forest, and each second equals one year. Watch their numbers and the graph of the last 16 years. You can remove the lynx or restart everything.
A:adimlar.7.gorev.bulgular.0.yazi: Watch one cycle and see which one peaks first.
A:adimlar.7.gorev.bulgular.0.tamam: The hares peaked first, and the lynx peaked after them.
A:adimlar.7.gorev.bulgular.1.yazi: Remove the lynx and see whether the hares grow forever.
A:adimlar.7.gorev.bulgular.1.tamam: The hares did not grow forever. They grew fast but stopped around 2000 when food ran short. Even without predators, environmental resistance limits growth and an S curve forms.
A:adimlar.7.gorev.bulgular.2.yazi: Bring back the lynx and watch a new cycle.
A:adimlar.7.gorev.bulgular.2.tamam: Facing many hares, the lynx multiplied quickly and reduced the hares. Then they declined too, and the cycle began again.
A:kapanis.0: Births and immigrants increase a population, while deaths and emigrants decrease it.
A:kapanis.1: Even at the same density, the distribution can be clumped, uniform or random.
A:kapanis.2: Unlimited resources give a J curve and limited resources an S curve. Growth is fastest around K/2.
A:kapanis.3: Epidemics and competition are density-dependent factors. Frost and floods are density-independent.
A:kapanis.4: The predator's numbers peak after the prey's. Of two species sharing the same limited resource, one is excluded.
